_meta.translationStatus: English draft; NGO educator sign-off pending. All baskets, savings and rates are fictional assumptions, not current prices, forecasts or product recommendations.

hook.1: Mira: My fictional savings have grown. Will they still buy the same rice, dal and vegetables?
hook.2: Mira: Interest is money earned on savings.
hook.3: Mira: Purchasing power means what money can buy, not just the number on a balance. Rising prices can reduce it.

choices.more: Buys more of this basket than at the start
choices.same: Buys the same amount of this basket as at the start
choices.less: Buys less of this basket than at the start

lesson.title: Same money, changing price tags
lesson.prompt: Simulated rice, dal and vegetable basket: ₹1,000 at the start. Assumption: basket prices rise 10% a year. Assumption: your cash earns 0% a year and stays ₹1,000. Move the slider through 2 years and compare the price tags. At the end, what can that unchanged cash buy?
lesson.hint1: Keep the goods and their quantities the same when comparing prices over time.
lesson.hint2: The basket price rises but the cash stays unchanged. Can the cash still cover the whole basket?
lesson.explanation: Under these assumptions, the same money buys less when the basket costs more. Its nominal amount is unchanged, but its purchasing power has fallen.

decision.title: A bigger balance at the market
decision.prompt: Mira starts with ₹1,000, enough for the same rice, dal and vegetable basket. Assumption: basket prices rise 6% a year. Assumption: savings grow 4% a year, compounded annually, with no deposits, withdrawals, fees or tax. After 3 years her savings are ₹1,124.86. Move the basket across the years. Compared with the start, what can her savings buy at the end?
decision.hint1: Compare the balance with the price of the same basket, not only with the starting balance.
decision.hint2: Assumption: savings grow 4% a year, slower than the assumed basket price rise of 6% a year. Which grows faster?
decision.explanation: Under these assumptions, savings grow in rupees but buy less of the basket. A higher nominal balance alone does not show higher purchasing power.

consequence.basket: After 3 years, the basket price has risen from ₹1,000 to ₹1,191.02. Assumption: prices rise 6% a year.
consequence.savings: Savings have grown from ₹1,000 to ₹1,124.86. Assumption: growth is 4% a year, compounded annually, without deposits, withdrawals, fees or tax.
consequence.gap: The savings are ₹66.16 short of the same basket. The bigger balance still buys less of it.
consequence.explanation: Money's number is not its purchasing power. When savings grow slower than prices, their purchasing power falls. This is a fictional comparison, not a forecast or a recommendation to buy any product.

school.title: Try a school-supplies basket
school.prompt: A different fictional basket of notebooks, pencils and paper costs ₹600 at the start. Assumption: these prices rise 5% a year. Assumption: cash earns 0% a year and stays ₹600. Move forward 2 years. Compared with the start, what can this cash buy?
school.hint1: Purchasing power is about goods you can afford, not whether the cash number changed.
school.hint2: The cash is unchanged while this basket becomes more expensive.
school.explanation: Under these assumptions, unchanged cash buys less of the school-supplies basket because its price rises.

cleaning.title: Try a cleaning-supplies basket
cleaning.prompt: A different fictional basket of soap and cleaning cloths costs ₹800 at the start. Assumption: these prices rise 8% a year. Assumption: savings grow 10% a year, compounded annually, with no deposits, withdrawals, fees or tax. After 2 years the savings are ₹968. Move the basket across 2 years. Compared with the start, what can these savings buy?
cleaning.hint1: Compare these savings with this basket's price before choosing.
cleaning.hint2: Assumption: savings grow 10% a year, faster than the assumed basket price rise of 8% a year.
cleaning.explanation: Under these assumptions, the savings grow faster than this basket's price, so they buy more of it. Rising prices do not always mean growing savings buy less.

nominal_vs_real.review: Your choice: the selected purchasing-power comparison does not match this basket and balance. Safer choice: compare the money with the price of the same basket at the same time. Concept: nominal amount is the number of rupees; purchasing power is what they buy. Savings growing slower than basket prices buy less; savings growing faster buy more, under the stated assumptions. Why it matters: savings that grow slower than prices can leave a planned purchase out of reach, even with a bigger balance.
